subtype: Approach: trial and error with version control [Action]
passage: When I first learned to code I was terrified of breaking things. My files felt like glass. Then a senior showed me how to work with branches, and it changed how I learned. Now I make a branch for every experiment, whatever it is. I try the risky thing. If it works, I keep it; if it collapses, I go back to the last save in one command. I commit every time something small works, even an ugly thing. Once I deleted a whole folder by mistake and was back in a minute. I am Akash, and I am still not brave, but the mistakes cost so little now that I try more things. — Akash

qa.q: What do I make for every experiment, according to Akash?
qa.a: Akash makes a branch for every experiment.

qa.q: How did Akash feel about breaking things at first?
qa.a: Akash was terrified of breaking things, feeling that the files were like glass.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Akash add to make the experiments teach more, and why?
qa.a: Akash could write a short note with each commit about what was tried, because a record of experiments shows what worked instead of only how to undo.

qa.q: How might a senior who taught Akash the method see this?
qa.a: The senior showed the branch idea and would probably be pleased to hear it changed Akash's habits, since the fear of breaking things has shrunk.

grounding: Shows experimenting on a separate branch with frequent saves so that a mistake can be undone easily and trying things stays cheap.

subtype: Approach: trial and error with version control [Action]
passage:
Supervisor's note – Kiran, week 3
Mridul is new to our web team and to the styling framework we use. On Monday I said: break things, but in a branch. Today I watched how that went.
Mridul made a branch called 'try-layout', changed the page grid and committed, changed the colours and committed, then tried a bold idea with floating side menus. The whole page collapsed into one long column. There was a short 'oh no', then Mridul went back one commit, and the page was fine again in under a minute.
By five o'clock the branch had fourteen small commits, two dead ends, and one layout that honestly looks better than ours. Mridul asked for a review. I have asked for the dead ends to be listed in the review notes too, since they teach the rest of us something.

qa.q: How many small commits did the branch have by five o'clock?
qa.a: Fourteen small commits, with two dead ends.

qa.q: What does Mridul's short 'oh no' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests a moment of alarm, quickly replaced by calm, because going back one commit fixed the page in under a minute.

qa.q: What else could keep Mridul's experiments cheap next time?
qa.a: Write a one-line message with each commit saying what was tried, so it is easy to see which step broke things and go back to it.

qa.q: How might the rest of the web team see the listed dead ends?
qa.a: They may be grateful, since seeing what did not work saves them from trying the same ideas.

grounding: Shows a new team member experimenting in a branch with frequent commits, so a broken layout is undone in a minute.

passage:
Wed, 11:40 pm
Big day for Jaya the chaos coder. I finally listened to Preeti and put my little game under version control before touching the new game engine. Preeti said, 'Make a branch, then go wild.' So I did.
Tried adding gravity: commit. Tried letting the player jump twice: commit. Tried a fancy shadow effect I saw somewhere, and the whole game went black and wouldn't start. Old me would have panicked and spent the night retyping from memory. Tonight I just went back two commits. Two minutes, and it ran again 😅
I did nine experiments today and threw away four. None of them cost me more than a few minutes. Honestly, this is the first time trying weird stuff felt safe instead of scary.
Tomorrow: ask Preeti how to merge the good ones back into the main branch.

qa.q: How many experiments did Jaya do today, and how many were thrown away?
qa.a: Jaya did nine experiments today and threw away four.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel about trying weird ideas today, compared with before?
qa.a: Jaya felt safe instead of scared, and relieved, since going back two commits took two minutes instead of a night of retyping.

qa.q: What small step would help Jaya tomorrow?
qa.a: Ask Preeti how to merge, as planned, and first check that the good experiments still run together before bringing them into the main branch.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel on hearing how the day went?
qa.a: Preeti would likely be pleased that the advice worked and that Jaya now feels free to explore.

grounding: Shows a learner experimenting in a branch and committing often, so a broken change is undone in minutes and exploring stays cheap.
